title: Two ways (Psalm 1)
hookLine: a tree planted by running waters, and chaff that blows away

lines: A GREEN TREE IN A DRY SUMMER.
cards: A dry summer. The lawns go brown and the hills turn to straw, but the trees along the river stay green. From a distance you can see where the water runs, because the trees follow it.
Their roots found something the rest of the field can't reach. Now the dust at the edge of a parking lot on a windy day, lifting, scattering, landing nowhere.
The first psalm, the one that opens the whole book, sets those two pictures side by side and says: there are two ways to live.

teach.b: Psalm 1 has no title and no author's name. It stands at the entrance like a sign over a door.

In the Douay-Rheims it opens: "Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the chair of pestilence." Listen to the verbs: walked, stood, sat.
A slow slide, from passing by, to stopping, to settling in. Then the other way.
That person's will, the Douay says, is in the law of the Lord, "and on his law he shall meditate day and night." The Hebrew word for meditate doesn't mean silent thinking.

It means to murmur, to mutter under your breath, the same word used for a dove cooing or a lion growling over its catch. Meditating, in the psalms, is saying the words over and over, half aloud, like chewing.
And that person is "like a tree which is planted near the running waters", bearing fruit in its season, its leaf not falling. Notice planted: somebody put it there, on purpose, near the water.
Then: "Not so the wicked, not so: but like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth."
In the Hebrew the picture is chaff, the husks blown off the threshing floor; the Latin, and the Douay after it, made it dust. Either way it weighs nothing and has nowhere to land.
The psalm doesn't say one way is easy and the other hard. It says one has roots.

how: Psalm 1 opens the psalter, and Catholics pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it as a responsorial psalm at Mass; many who begin reading the psalms start here, as at a front door.

o: a rooted life, or a life blown about
the road to heaven and the road to hell

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: a slow slide into the wrong way

s: in the Douay, the wicked are like chaff
the Hebrew says chaff, but the Latin and the Douay say dust, which the wind drives away.

games.q: the psalm describes three steps into the wrong way. what's the order?
games.why: walked in the counsel of the ungodly, stood in the way of sinners, sat in the chair of pestilence: from passing by, to stopping, to settling in.

practice: Stand by water if there's a river, a fountain or even a running tap nearby, or picture a tree on a riverbank, its roots going slowly down toward the water under the ground.

Ask where your own roots are drinking from these days: what feeds you, and what just blows through? If you pray, murmur one line under your breath, the way the psalm means, blessed is the man; if you don't, just stay with the tree.

wordCard.voice: Two ways. The first psalm's choice: a tree with roots near water, or dust with nowhere to land. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: blessed, or happy. the first word of the first psalm.

carryVoice: Your line: roots near water. A tree planted by the water, not dust on the wind. Until tomorrow.
